title: A day in Mohenjo-daro
deck: Forty thousand people, 4,500 years ago, with wells, drains and dice. Nobody can read a word they wrote. Walk through one day using only what was dug up.
kidDeck: 4,500 years ago, this was one of the biggest cities in the world. We cannot read its writing. But we can tell a lot about a day there from what people left behind.

scenes.title: A day in *Mohenjo-daro*
text: Mohenjo-daro was built around 2500 BCE beside the Indus, in today's Sindh in Pakistan. With at least 40,000 people it was one of the world's earliest major cities, as old as the cities of Egypt and Mesopotamia.
Its people left signs on seals and pots, but nobody has deciphered them. So this is a day reconstructed from walls, wells and things lost in the dust. Where we do not know, the story says so.
kid: 4,500 years ago, a great city stood beside the Indus River, in what is now Pakistan. About 40,000 people lived there.
We cannot read their writing, so nobody knows their names or their stories. But we can see their houses, their wells and their toys. Let us walk through one day.

scenes.title: Morning: water from the well
text: The day begins with water. Households, or small groups of them, drew it from their own wells, and the city has a great number of them. The central marketplace had a large well of its own.
kid: The day starts with water. Most houses had their own well, or shared one with the neighbours.

sources.title: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

scenes.note: The times of day in this story are a way of telling it. The evidence does not record a schedule.

scenes.title: A house around a courtyard
text: Most houses were built of fired brick around an inner courtyard, with doors that opened onto side lanes. Some had rooms that seem to have been set aside for bathing.
Several courtyard houses had a washing platform and a toilet. It was flushed with a jar of water, which ran through a clay pipe into a shared brick drain.
kid: Houses were built of baked bricks around an open courtyard. The door opened onto a side lane.
Many houses had a place to wash and even a toilet. You flushed it by pouring in a jar of water.

sources.title: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

img.alt: Excavated ruins of Mohenjo-daro, with the Great Bath in the foreground.
img.caption: Excavated ruins of Mohenjo-daro, with the Great Bath in the foreground.

scenes.title: Streets on a grid, drains under cover
text: Step outside and the city is planned: straight-sided buildings laid out on a grid. Waste water from the houses ran into covered drains along the major streets. The drains had openings at regular intervals for cleaning and inspection.
These are among the first known examples of city sanitation anywhere.
kid: The streets were straight and crossed each other like the lines on squared paper. Dirty water ran away through covered drains beside the street. These are some of the earliest city drains known anywhere.

sources.title: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

scenes.title: To market
text: The city had a central marketplace. Traders used standardised weights, and small stamp seals, most only two or three centimetres across, cut with signs and pressed into clay.
More than 400 different signs are known from about 4,000 inscribed objects. Most inscriptions are extremely short, and whether the signs record a language at all is still argued over.
kid: In the middle of the city was a market. Traders used weights that were the same everywhere. They also used little seals, only two or three centimetres across, to press a mark into clay.
The seals carry signs that look like writing. Nobody today can read them.

img.alt: A modern impression of an Indus seal with a line of five signs, photographed at the British Museum.
img.caption: A modern impression of an Indus seal with a line of five signs, photographed at the British Museum.

scenes.title: The bead-makers' supplies
text: Craftspeople depended on things from far away. Trade networks reached distant sources of raw materials, among them lapis lazuli and other stones for bead-making. Copper came from Rajasthan and from as far as Oman.
Goods probably moved in bullock carts like those still seen across South Asia, and in small flat-bottomed boats on the river.
kid: The city's craftspeople made beads from coloured stones. Some of the stones, and the copper for tools, came from very far away. They probably travelled in ox carts and in flat boats on the river.
scenes.note: The arrow links a source named in the article to the city. The route is not known.

scenes.title: Children's corner
text: People here made toys and games. Terracotta figurines of cows, bears, monkeys and dogs have been found, most of them probably toys. So have cubical dice with one to six holes on their faces, found at Mohenjo-daro itself.
kid: Children here had toys. Little clay cows, bears, monkeys and dogs have been found. So have dice, with one to six dots on the sides, just like the dice you know.

scenes.title: Afternoon at the Great Bath
text: On the high mound called the Citadel stood the Great Bath: a pool about 12 metres by 7 and up to 2.4 metres deep. Its floor was made watertight with finely fitted bricks set in gypsum plaster, and its sides were sealed with a thick layer of bitumen.
Most scholars agree it was used for special religious functions in which water purified the bathers. No text says so.
kid: On a high mound stood a big brick pool, 12 metres long, with steps leading down into it. The builders sealed it with tar so it would not leak.
Most experts think people bathed here for religious reasons. But we cannot be sure.

img.alt: The Great Bath on the citadel mound of Mohenjo-daro.
img.caption: The Great Bath on the citadel mound of Mohenjo-daro.

scenes.title: A girl in bronze
text: One citizen has a face, though not a name. A bronze figure only 10.5 centimetres tall, cast by the lost-wax method some time between about 2300 and 1750 BC, shows a young woman standing with one hand on her hip. She wears 24 or 25 bangles on her left arm and four on her right.
She is called the Dancing Girl. Whether she is dancing is a guess.
kid: One small bronze statue shows us a person from the city. She is a girl, standing with one hand on her hip, with bangles all the way up one arm. The statue is only about 10 centimetres tall.
People call her the Dancing Girl, but nobody knows if she was dancing.

img.alt: The Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro, bronze, about 10.5 cm tall, in the National Museum, New Delhi.
img.caption: The Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro, bronze, about 10.5 cm tall, in the National Museum, New Delhi.

scenes.title: Evening: who was in charge?
text: Who planned the grid and the drains? There is no conclusive evidence of palaces or temples. Some houses were larger than others, but Indus cities are remarkable for their apparent, if relative, egalitarianism.
Who governed, and how, is unknown.
kid: Somebody must have planned the streets and the drains. But no palace for a king has been found, and no great temple. Some houses were larger than others, but the city seems to have been unusually equal. Who ran it is still a mystery.

scenes.title: The city empties
text: The mature Indus civilisation lasted from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. Then it went into decline, and by about 1700 BCE Mohenjo-daro had been abandoned, along with the other large Indus cities.
kid: The city lasted for hundreds of years. Then the cities of the Indus declined. By about 1700 BCE Mohenjo-daro had been abandoned.

scenes.title: Found again
text: The ruins lay undocumented for around 3,700 years. In 1919–1920 R. D. Banerji, an officer of the Archaeological Survey of India, visited the mound. He came to see what he took for a Buddhist stupa, and found a flint scraper that convinced him the place was far older.
The name Mohenjo-daro is Sindhi, and means "Mound of the Dead Men". What its own people called their city is not known.
kid: For about 3,700 years nobody knew the city was there. Then, about a hundred years ago, an Indian archaeologist named R. D. Banerji visited the mound and realised it was very, very old.
We still do not know what the people who lived there called their city.

q: Why do we not know the names of people from Mohenjo-daro?
options: They had no writing at all
quiz.why: The signs on the Indus seals have never been deciphered, so no names or stories can be read.

q: What ran beside the main streets of the city?
quiz.why: Waste water from the houses was channelled into covered drains along the major streets.

q: Which of these toys has been found in the city?
quiz.why: Cubical dice with one to six holes on their faces were found at Mohenjo-daro.
